html:
projectionist — the NAS media pipeline as one service

Today the pipeline is a set of Python 3.8 scripts on the DS423+. DSM Task Scheduler runs some of them, and the owner runs the others by hand. projectionist replaces them, one at a time, with one Go service in one container. The service runs each step ("stage") on its own schedule, keeps its state in SQLite, and is observable over HTTP. A projectionist runs the show from the booth and stays out of the audience's way. Here, that means every disruptive job pauses while anyone but the owner is watching.

                          DS423+ (DSM 7.4.1, kernel 4.4, J4125 + UHD 600)
 ┌──────────────────────────── container "projectionist" (host network) ───────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                                                 │
 │  scheduler ── one goroutine per stage; cadence + optional window ("02:00-08:00" Pacific);      │
 │      │        never two copies of a stage at once                                               │
 │      ▼                                                                                          │
 │  Runner ── StartRun ─► stage.Run(ctx, env, &report) ─► FinishRun(outcome) ─► logs + metrics    │
 │      │                       │                                                                  │
 │      │            ┌──────────┼──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐                    │
 │      │            ▼          ▼              ▼               ▼              ▼                    │
 │      │        gpu-guard   remote4k    details    subtitles    rename   ingest*  jf-sync*        │
 │      │            │          │                                                                  │
 │      │   env: Plex client · Jellyfin client · viewers.Gate (pause rule) · probe (ffprobe cache)│
 │      │        fsx (renameat2 NOREPLACE, FICLONE, dir fsync) · store · FFmpeg paths              │
 │      ▼                                                                                          │
 │  SQLite /state/projectionist.db (WAL): runs · kv · events · probe_cache · <stage>_* tables      │
 │  HTTP 127.0.0.1:8097: GET /health (503 on alert/error) · GET /metrics (Prometheus text)         │
 └──────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
        │ /dev/dri/        │ http 127.0.0.1      │ /volume1/media   │ ro: Plex AppData,
        │ renderD128       │ :32400  :8096       │ (only rw media mount) │ Plex package, scripts/
        ▼                  ▼                     ▼                       ▼
   GPU (QSV/VAAPI)    Plex · Jellyfin      Movies/ TV/ _archive/    Preferences.xml (token),
                                            .projectionist/ (work)   Plex log, transcoder
   DSM task "projectionist health": curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8097/health  → DSM failure e-mail
                                                                    (* = stage not ported yet)

The pieces

Concern Design Code
Stages One interface: Name(), Run(ctx, env, *Report) error. A stage must be idempotent: a rerun after a crash finishes the work and never repeats a side effect. A stage stops when ctx is cancelled. Report.Alert and Report.Count give the outcome and the metrics. internal/stage
Scheduler Per stage: every, optional window in the config time zone (Pacific; it may wrap past midnight). The next run is computed from the last run's start time read from SQLite, so a restart does not rerun a stage early. Each stage has its own goroutine, so a 6 h encode delays only itself. internal/scheduler
Trigger Env.Trigger(name) runs a stage soon (inside its window); triggers that arrive while it runs or waits give exactly one more run. The watcher stage calls it: inotify on the library and finished downloads, a top-level folder that stayed quiet for 3 min triggers the reconcilers once, and a 15 min mtime sweep catches lost events. Plex and Jellyfin are not involved. internal/scheduler, internal/stages/watcher
State SQLite in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL: at most one fsync per transaction commit. Shared tables: runs, kv (per-stage JSON state), events (per-item history), probe_cache, library_changes (a running total per stage of the changes Plex's database records, which the health stage reads). A stage owns its own <stage>_* tables. Pure Go driver (modernc), so the binary stays static. internal/store
Resume Every run is a row. A run a shutdown or restart cuts off (its context cancelled) is recorded "interrupted"; a row without finished_at means the process died mid-run. Neither is an outcome: /health shows the last finished run's, so a restart by itself neither raises nor clears an alert. A cut-off run that already raised alerts is recorded "alert", because some alerts are raised only once (a stored marker says the owner was told). The stage resumes from its own state, e.g. remote4k redoes the film because no copy exists yet.
Logs log/slog on stderr, key=value (or JSON), UTC RFC 3339 timestamps, always event=<snake_case> plus fields (stage=, item=, duration_ms=, err=). Docker's json-file driver rotates them at 10 MB × 5. internal/obs
Health /health answers 503 while, for any stage, the run in progress has raised an alert (at once, not when the run ends), or the latest finished run raised an alert or failed and no later run has been running for 30 min without one. A run that drains a backlog can last many hours: on 2026-10-07 an old subtitles alert held /health at 503, and the owner's inbox under an e-mail every 15 min, for ~12 h of a clean run. Each stage's run_alerts in the body lists the alerts its run in progress has raised so far. A one-line DSM task (curl -fsS .../health, every 15 min, "e-mail on failure") keeps DSM's existing e-mail as the alert channel, with no new credentials. /metrics exports runs, alerts, items, last-run time and duration per stage. internal/server
Secrets Never in env vars and never in the config. The Plex token is read from Preferences.xml (read-only mount) on every request and sent as a header, never in a URL. The Jellyfin key, the TMDB read token and v3 key, and the fanart.tv key arrive as compose secrets under /run/secrets/ (read-only) and are read per request; the TMDB token and the fanart.tv key travel in headers. A rotated secret therefore needs no restart, and nothing logs it. internal/plex, internal/jellyfin, internal/tmdb, internal/fanart
Sources Facts come from the files: ffprobe, folder and file names, the rename logs. Identity, episode lists, specials, collections, external ids and images come from TMDB v3 directly (one client per process: 40 req/s token bucket, 10 s timeout, 429/5xx retried twice, 24 h response cache in http_cache), artwork also from fanart.tv. Subtitles come from subtitle providers. internal/probe, internal/library, internal/tmdb, internal/fanart
Plex and Jellyfin Sinks only; both APIs stall during library scans. Allowed: writes of state that lives in the app (preferences, posters, collections, watched state), mapping a TMDB id to the app's item id, the viewer gate's live sessions, the webhooks/events the apps push, lists the owner keeps there as requests (remote4k's "Remote 4K"), and upkeep of the app itself (the health stage times Plex's hubs and runs its Optimize Database; the answers are not read). Every call is time-bounded and a slow app never fails a run. Never a data source: no Jellyfin RemoteSearch/RemoteImages/ProviderIds, no Plex metadata or subtitle search, no live app DB, no rescan requests (Jellyfin gets one /Library/Media/Updated) but one: the subtitles stage asks Plex for a partial scan of each folder it wrote a sidecar to, which Plex's own watcher does not add. internal/plex, internal/jellyfin
ffmpeg The image carries /usr/lib/jellyfin-ffmpeg (8.1.2-Jellyfin, with the iHD/i965 VA drivers), copied from the same Jellyfin image tag the NAS runs. That is the same build Jellyfin itself uses. /dev/dri/renderD128 is passed through, and the container joins group 937 (videodriver). Encodes use QSV (-init_hw_device vaapi=va:/dev/dri/renderD128 -init_hw_device qsv=qs@va, hevc_qsv/h264_qsv). The GPU self-test also runs Plex's own transcoder (read-only mount) as the Plex user, via VAAPI. Dockerfile, gpu-guard
Pause rule viewers.Gate: count Plex and Jellyfin sessions not owned by owners (the owner's viewing never blocks a job). Use WaitIdle before moving files and poll Count to SIGSTOP/SIGCONT a long encode. If the count cannot be read, the gate treats it as busy. internal/viewers
Self-healing The health stage probes Plex, Jellyfin, qBittorrent, the Cloudflare hostnames and the containers every 5 min. After 3 failed runs it alerts. It restarts a container only if the container is in restartable (default: none, so a restart is opt-in), the failure is one a restart cures (no answer, 5xx, Docker "unhealthy"; never a refused key or a stopped container), nobody is playing on Jellyfin, and the last restart was ≥ 1 h ago (a shorter restart_cooldown is refused). "Nobody is playing" is a /Sessions count; when /Sessions does not answer, the restart waits, unless Jellyfin answered none of that run's requests. A restart is three steps, never Docker's one-call restart: stop with a 120 s grace before SIGKILL, start, then poll the service's own probe (Jellyfin: /System/Info/Public) every 5 s until it answers, for at most 5 min. On 2026-10-05 docker restart SIGKILLed a Jellyfin still cancelling a scan after its 10 s grace and never ran the start half, so no Docker answer is taken as proof: while the poll fails, a container still exited and not started since the request is started again, and a service that has not answered after 5 min is alerted as a FAILED restart; its failure streak is kept, so every later run alerts until the service answers, and the cooldown holds a second restart. It writes the restart to SQLite, with that restart's own time, before it sends it; a shutdown never cancels the stop or the start, only the wait. If the process dies between them anyway, the next run starts the container: it last started before the recorded restart and stopped within a minute past the stop request's 7 min deadline (Docker 24 SIGKILLs when a stop's client gives up, so that deadline outlives the grace). A container the owner stops is left stopped. Every Docker call carries a deadline, so a wedged dockerd cannot hang the stage. The Docker socket is root on the host, so the allow-list is what limits it. It also watches Plex's speed: on 2026-10-05 a database fragmented by mass edits took the Movies tab 26.8 s to load cold, and Plex's Optimize Database brought it to 17 ms. Every run times the Movies and Home hubs (projectionist_health_plex_hub_seconds). After 3 runs in a row slower than plex_slow (5 s), or more than plex_batch (500) library changes since the last optimize (details notes, rename moves, Plex collection edits, counted in library_changes), it sends one optimize inside plex_optimize_window (03:00-06:00) while nobody but the owner watches, at most once per 24 h, follows it in Plex's /activities, times the hubs again, and alerts while they stay slow. internal/stages/health
Least privilege Root inside the container, because files must keep their owners. All capabilities are dropped except CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, KILL, SETUID and SETGID. Also: no-new-privileges, read-only root filesystem, 1 GB memory cap, cpu_shares: 256 (Plex and Jellyfin win any contention). The only writable media mount is /volume1/media. compose.yaml

File-level operations (measured on this NAS, 2026-10-05)

A throwaway probe in scratch folders of two non-media shares (deleted afterwards) gave these results:

Operation Result on DSM kernel 4.4.302+, btrfs Consequence
renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE) Works: EEXIST onto an existing file or folder, ok otherwise. It also works on ext4. Every library move is one atomic syscall that cannot overwrite (fsx.RenameNoReplace). The old check-then-rename race is gone. A link+unlink fallback exists for filesystems without the flag.
FICLONE reflink Works within a share and across shares. Fails with EXDEV onto ext4 /tmp. Copies on the volume are instant and use no space (fsx.Clone, with a byte-copy fallback).
hardlink / rename across shares EXDEV (each share is its own btrfs subvolume: st_dev 42/40/43). Within a share, it works. Hardlink ingest works only if qBittorrent downloads into the Plex Media share. From another share, ingest must use a reflink clone instead (just as instant, and the copy is independent of the torrent's file). Work directories live in the destination's share. remote4k publishes with one rename from Plex Media/.projectionist/remote4k.
Synology ACL A plain mkdir or create under a folder that has its ACL inherits it. chmod strips it; chown keeps it. This is the root cause of the pilot bug ("Plex marked items deleted"). The executor did chown+chmod on each new folder, then repaired the damage with one synoacltool subprocess per folder. The Go stages never chmod, so they need no ACL work and no synoacltool, which the container does not have anyway.
Durability One fsync per unit, not per op. The rename executor appends all intended ops of a unit to its undo log (undo.tsv, apply_ops.py's TSV format) and fsyncs it once (the "log before acting" rule). It then performs the renames, fsyncs each folder that unit touched once (fsx.SyncDir), and appends unit-done. A unit stopped half-way is finished by the next run, which re-plans from the disk (src gone and dst present means done). Undo logs its undone rows the same way, one fsync per unit. The old executor's ~18 ops/s came from a per-op fsync of undo.tsv plus a synoacltool exec per new folder. Both costs disappear here.

Where Rust earns its place: one vendored tool

Every stage so far is bound by I/O or subprocesses: ffmpeg/ffprobe, HTTP (TMDB, Plex, Jellyfin), renames on a RAID5 volume. Go reaches the needed syscalls directly (renameat2, FICLONE, setpriority through x/sys) and ships as a single 12 MB static binary (stripped). The CPU-heavy candidates are small:

  • subtitle alignment against a PGS track: cue-time fitting over 3 frame-rate ratios, milliseconds per title;
  • hashing for deduplication: Go's SHA-256 uses the J4125's SHA extensions.

Rust earns a crate when a stage needs a library only Rust has, or when a profile on the J4125 shows a ≥2× wall-time win on a stage's critical path. The first case is subtitle sync to the speech in the audio (voice-activity detection plus split-aware alignment), which the subtitles stage's alignment queue needs for titles without an English image track, and to rescue a downloaded subtitle whose timing the image track rejects (a cut or a drift the caption fit cannot follow). A subtitle made for the file's own release, or one that fits an English .en.idx sidecar's caption times, is written without it and without reading the video; one the sampled fit (four short windows of the video, its voice-activity detection a level-onset score in Go) places is written without it too: alass, built from a pinned commit as a static musl binary in the image (/usr/local/bin/alass) and exec'd by the stage.

Migration: one script at a time, deleted at its cutover

A Go stage replaces a Python script only when it matches that script on the gate below. The old script and its DSM task are deleted in the same cutover, so there is never a window where both act. The same cutover deploys the image, enables the stage's [stages.<name>] table, and imports any legacy state (gpu-guard reads gpu_guard.state.json once, so the first run does not re-alert on old log lines).

# Stage Replaces Acceptance gate
1 gpu-guard scripts/gpu_guard.py, DSM task 8 Ported. Table tests on every decision, plus a fake-server run: drift repaired, each transcode alerted once, log offset kept across rotation, self-test only when idle and once a day, a hung Plex costs 5 s per call and only a pin that cannot be written back alerts ("GPU pin lost"). On the NAS: projectionist run gpu-guard gives the same alert set as the Python run in the same window (none expected), and both GPU self-tests pass (>100 frames), also with Plex unreachable.
2 remote4k scripts/remote4k.py, DSM task 9 Ported. Requests are the union of the Plex playlist and Jellyfin playlists/collections named "Remote 4K"; source facts come from ffprobe only. Table tests (selection, encode arguments) and an end-to-end fake run (real SIGSTOP/SIGCONT, DV5 skip, union deduped, no Plex rescan, rerun does nothing, either app hung leaves its half empty; each half, and each of its requests, waits up to list_timeout, 30 s, as a busy Plex took over 5 s). On the NAS: an empty list does nothing (also with Plex unreachable); for one playlist film, the Go ffmpeg argument list equals the Python's, the copy's ffprobe colour tags and HDR10 match, and a guest session pauses the encode.
3 details rename/write_details.py For every video, the .details text equals the Python output on every field from the rename log. Probe-derived fields (codec, bit depth, HDR, audio, subtitles) agree on ≥99.5 %, and every difference is listed with its cause (Plex analysis vs ffprobe).
4 subtitles scripts/sub_stats.py, scripts/subfetch2.py Ported (providers called directly, never Plex: OpenSubtitles legacy REST, Gestdown, a film site; SubSource and Subdl with keys; OpenSubtitles.com with a key and a free user's login). Build-tagged replay harness (gate_test.go) against the scripts' own code on the NAS, rerun at the final commit: the sub_stats TSV byte-identical on 378 real subtitle files; the OpenSubtitles hash on 20 videos; align/retime numbers on 30 real (reference, candidate) pairs taken from the Python job's own decisions; download decoding on 325 real files under 7 declared encodings (2,600 rows, cp1250 included). subfetch2.py v8's OpenSubtitles quota is ported (8 min between downloads, 180 per 24 h, a refused download or a quota header at 10 stops downloads and searches for 24 h, kept in the store and imported once from the script's own quota.csv/downloads.csv). End to end in scratch with Gestdown and the film site (OpenSubtitles was denying the NAS IP): 10 of 20 titles that had no English text got a subtitle, and the 7 with English image captions sit a median 108-282 ms from them (median 220 ms). A downloaded subtitle the captions reject is rescued by alass when its alignment then fits within 300 ms. Never overwrites (O_EXCL). Cheap first (the owner's ruling, 2026-10-05: no audio or video work for a subtitle that can simply be downloaded): a video whose probe cache or .details note names an embedded English text track already has English subtitles (the players show it, and the audit counts it so) and is not searched (4,637 of the 6,171 videos lacking an English sidecar on 2026-10-05, about 10 TB); since the owner's ruling of 2026-10-07 the extraction pass writes that track as <video>.en.srt, one read of the whole file each; a candidate made for the file's own release (its original name's group, from the .details note or the rename logs, with no source, resolution, service, edition or episode contradicting it; or an OpenSubtitles file-hash match labelled with the title) is written without opening the video once cheapCheck passes on the note's or the probe cache's duration and frame rate (last cue within the video and at most 8 % before its end). Gestdown and the film site are searched first; OpenSubtitles last, for its hash match, or for any candidate only when no other provider has one; while it is out (its 180-a-day quota) it holds back only a title no other provider has a candidate for, and its 128 KiB hash is read only when it is about to search. Every other title waits in subtitles_queue, aligned (caption stream, else alass, rescue included) only while nobody but the owner watches and at most align_per_day (20) titles in any 24 h, at nice 19 and the lowest best-effort I/O priority; its candidates are downloaded one at a time until one fits, an alignment counts against the cap only as it starts reading the video, and a title that needs alass while alass is out waits without spending a search, a download or the cap. Gate (cb22643) on 30 sampled videos lacking English text subtitles (22 episodes, 8 films) plus 10 with an embedded English text track, Gestdown, the film site and OpenSubtitles listed with OpenSubtitles parked by its real quota wait: the 10 skipped, 2 release-matched, 23 queued, 5 deferred for OpenSubtitles (no other provider had a candidate), in 92 s, with 0 bytes read from any of the 40 (inotify saw no open of them, and no hash was read); a cap of 3 then aligned 3 with OpenSubtitles still parked (0.8-13.3 GB read each, a rescue reads twice; 4 downloads for 3 titles). Of the 2 release-matched, the one with English captions (Melancholia) sits a median 0 ms from them; alass would move them 114 and 44 ms. Sampled alignment (mode = "sampled", the default; careful, the rollback, is the queue alone). Every write is fitted to the video first, a release match first (fix/subs-defects: a release match trusted once its length fitted could sit 15.7 s off, The Game). Quick mode, which wrote any plausible subtitle the cheap check passed, is gone (its spot check: 4 of 5 such writes were 1.3-55 s off, and a written sidecar is never revisited). Per title, the first route that succeeds: (a) a release match once cheapCheck passes, no read; (b) a plausible candidate fitted to an English <stem>.en.idx sidecar's caption starts (its text only; one with a caption after the video's end is no timing), no read; (c) the sampled fit (sampled.go): 4 windows of 90 s, the first starting at 3 % of the runtime and the last ending at 97 %, read through the container's index (Matroska and MP4-family files only: an AVI's seek landed 1.3 s off 45 minutes in), from the English image track's packet times (one ffprobe -read_intervals showing every stream, with absolute ends: shown one track, ffprobe reads on to its next packet, the end of the file after the last caption; no image decoded) or else the voice band of the first audio track, its centre channel where the layout has one (one ffmpeg -ss per window, 16 kHz mono); a window without dialogue is replaced by the stretch next to it toward the middle, twice at most, and a helper whose reads pass 4 times its share of the file plus 64 MiB is killed (rchar polled every 20 ms) and the title queued. The candidate is fitted as t' = ratio*t + offset, ratio from 1, 25/23.976, 24/23.976, 25/24 and their inverses, and written retimed only when every window has evidence at the joint offset (6 matched caption starts and half of its captions, or an onset score 3.5 deviations above its others), the windows' own offsets lie within 0.3 s of each other, the ratio scores 1.4 times any other, and the stretch an outer window moved inward from holds at most 7 of its lines per skipped window; the history keeps the ratio, offset, each window's offset and evidence, those unseen lines, and the bytes read (rchar and read_bytes). What no check sees: the first and last 3 %, and a difference inside an edge window whose other part holds more evidence, at most 3 % plus 90 s at each end. The calibration behind those bars is calibrate_test.go (build tag calibrate: at the stage's layout, 11 titles with known timing, 0 of 256 wrong subtitles or other cuts passed, cuts at 8 % and 92 % among them). (d) the queue as above, only inside align_window (01:00-07:00): a run outside it, or inside it with the day's cap spent, asks the scheduler (Report.Wake) for a run when it may align next (the oldest counted alignment plus 24 h, while the window is still open; before, the 6 h cadence could land after 07:00 and lose the night). Gate (1c3e8da, on reflink clones in scratch, OpenSubtitles parked by its quota): the quick gate's 35, 34 drawn at random from the backlog (1,486 videos on 2026-10-05: 1,059 MKV, 427 MP4, no AVI) and 4 AVIs. 23 written (1 release match, 6 .idx fits, 16 sampled fits), 41 queued (the 4 AVIs among them), 9 deferred for OpenSubtitles; the sampled step read 53 titles and wrote 16 (9 of 25 by captions, 7 of 28 by speech). Every sampled write sits within 134 ms of an independent whole-file reference at the start, middle and end (the 9 caption fits against the complete caption track less the windows' captions; the 7 speech fits against alass, worst 116 ms); alass on the caption fits disagrees by up to 0.27 s on two (Double Indemnity, The Big Bang Theory S04E07). Each write timed for another cut from 8 % or 92 % of its runtime: 30 of 32 refused. Bytes read per sampled title, read_bytes as % of the file: MKV median 17 %, p95 38 %; MP4 median 24 %, p95 38 %; films median 7 %, episodes 32 % (four 90 s windows of a 22-minute episode are a quarter of it). 16.6 s per title (median; p95 44 s). The five subtitles quick mode wrote unverified in its spot check: The Place Beyond the Pines (24/23.976, +1.0 s: not another cut), Modern Family S02E06 (25/23.976) and Entourage come out within 24 ms of their whole caption tracks; Jackie Brown (19 end-credit lines in a stretch no window read) and Generation Kill (its captions too sparse in a window) go to the queue. Cutover: subfetch2.py goes; sub_stats.py stays until autorename (row 6) is ported, because autorename.py runs it for each dropped folder and the rename planner reads that run's TSV. Align workers (align_remote_lanes, default 0 = off): projectionist align-worker on another machine reaches the listener over SSH (loopback callers only): a forwarded port, or -via, a relay its ssh login runs on the NAS, whose sshd refuses port forwarding and leases the queue's titles while it has called in the last minute; the NAS streams only the tracks the alignment reads (-c copy into Matroska), downloads each candidate when the worker asks (the same quotas), and writes (O_EXCL) and records the worker's result after its own length check; the worker runs the stage's own alignment on its ffmpeg and alass. A lease without a result in 15 min ends and its title stays queued; with no worker connected the queue aligns on the NAS. Plex gets a partial scan of each new sidecar's folder (/library/sections/<id>/refresh?path=), kept for the next push when refused (each push stops at the first refusal or after 30 s); the first run queues once the folders of every sidecar written before.
5 rename planner + executor rename_engine.py, apply_ops.py Ported (also replaces autorename's matching). Identity from the names and TMDB directly (a tag in the name, then TMDB search under the acceptance rule, then _needs-review.txt); never from Plex, and never from the library's own folder names. Port check: on the recorded input TSVs, op/src/dst/reason equal the Python's for 21333/21334 rows; the other is intended: a subtitle of a special left for review stays beside it, where the Python archived it. A TMDB failure (identity, episode list or show details) leaves the show's unnumbered videos in place for the next run. History (undo.tsv, 13085 moves; original path in, identity from each destination's {tmdb-N} folder): 13084 byte-identical with the episode titles the Python planner had (the other row moved Ad Astra back out of _archive/samples, where a plan from before the is_main guard had put it); 13005 (99.389 %) with TMDB's episode titles, which production reads. The 79 extra differences are only TMDB's spelling of the episode title: 37 case or punctuation, 35 other words, 7 placeholder titles the planner drops. Episodes already named keep their own titles, so this renames nothing already in the library; it decides how new arrivals are spelled. Subtitle facts equal sub_stats.py on 3459/3459 real files. NAS sandbox (20 real folders, sparse files): apply; a second apply changes nothing; undo restores the tree exactly; a second undo writes nothing; apply after undo leaves what undo put back. Replay harness: internal/stages/rename/replay_test.go (-tags replay).
6 autorename rename/autorename.py Folded into rename: a new arrival is renamed once its folder has been quiet for quiet (10 min); an unmatched one goes to _needs-review.txt with TMDB's top 3 candidates. Its .details and subtitle queue belong to the details and subtitles stages, which read the disk.
7 ingest qBittorrent hook (in progress) Hardlink within the Plex Media share, reflink across shares. Same bytes and inode/extent sharing verified, zero extra space used, the torrent keeps seeding.
8 jfsync jellyfin/jf_mirror.py (watch half; collections and posters are their own stages) Watch state is projectionist's own record (internal/watch: Plex webhook, Jellyfin Webhook plugin, a one-time import per person of the newest Plex DB backup copy and of Jellyfin's played, resumable and rated items, and the Letterboxd diaries of the owner and of each of letterboxd's people (each under their own person), which the letterboxd stage records and never writes to an app itself; a Jellyfin push carries no rating), written to both apps field by field by this stage alone, last writer wins; listings and imports wait for non-owner viewers. On the NAS: dry-run counts per user and direction, an apply for the owner, a second run writes nothing, items spot-checked in both apps.
9 ssdmirror ssd-copy/fill.py Removed (owner, 2026-10-05). The SSD copy is a one-time copy for a friend, not pipeline work, so the stage is deleted and fill.py is not replaced.
10 backups backup_plex_db.sh, export_customizations.py PRAGMA integrity_check = ok on the copy. The exported file set equals the Python's.
11 posters posters/posters.py (ran on the Mac) Ported. Candidates from the shared TMDB and fanart.tv clients plus the owner's posters (from a Plex DB backup and its export; a newer export merges in, and its defaults never erase an upload or pick); judge = [llm.tasks.posters]'s vision model through the AI gateway, or the API of its own the task names (the bake-off, cmd/bakeoff, picks it), as many calls at once as [llm] in_flight allows, a $12 hard budget held per call at its worst case (an attempt whose answer was lost stays counted at its worst case). The owner's uploads and picks are never replaced (his picks are often deliberate alternative art, which the judge marks down against mainstream key art); Plex's default only by a candidate scored at least 2 points higher (1 is within the judge's noise). When these rules change, every title judged before is decided again from its stored scores, with no call. An owner poster that cannot be read (a truncated JPEG in the export) skips its title, which keeps the poster the apps show, with one alert, raised again only when that file changes. Each title's downloads, judge call and uploads wait while a guest watches; both apps always get the chosen image, and a failed Plex lock is retried without a second upload. Each outbox row remembers the app item it went to: a title an app lists under a new item after the daily listing (Jellyfin's id hashes the path, so any rename) gets its poster again. Jellyfin is listed one type at a time in pages; an app unlistable for sink_alert_after (72 h) alerts. Calls still in flight that fill the budget only defer judging; real spend at the cap alerts. A task the gateway keeps failing parks for the run with one alert; a billing refusal parks it with one alert, raised again only after a call has succeeded. The owner's own uploads go back without the EXIF mark, so a later export can tell them from the stage's. Secret ai_gateway_api_key (or the task's own key_file); read-only mount of backups/. Gate: the 12-title pilot in dry-run, each pick compared with the Python pilot's, under $0.10. Collections (the collections stage's desired set less the owner's 111, so the approved list and the director collections arrivals open): a franchise pools its TMDB collection's posters, fanart.tv's art for that collection (fanart.tv files it under /movies/<collection id>; its name must equal TMDB's) and its most acclaimed film's poster (the one this stage chose, when judged); a director pools Wikimedia Commons photos that depict the director's Wikidata item (from TMDB's external ids) or sit in a category Commons ties to it, then text hits naming them, on-set shots first, taking turns with TMDB's tagged images and portraits. One vision call per collection ([llm.tasks.collections]'s model) judges identity from captions and the director's films, never faces, prefers an on-set photo and boxes the director; the photo becomes a textless 1000x1500 poster (the owner's own director posters are textless photos; a wide photo keeps 4:5 of its context over a blurred backdrop). A director's best photo must score director_min_score (4), and a lone Commons text hit is judged, never taken unseen; otherwise the collection stays without a poster and alerts. Plex addresses a collection by name in the Movies section and locks it as type 18; Jellyfin by BoxSet name. The owner's collections are never a target whatever they are called (Plex: his file's ratingKeys; Jellyfin: the BoxSets the collections stage gave his posters), a first upload leaves a Plex collection poster someone else locked, and only this run's collections are sent. An empty pool is gathered again daily and alerts after 3 days. Own budget collection_budget_usd ($5) and own collection_dry_run (on unless set false). Plex uploads and locks count as library changes for health's optimize. Criterion: a film the Criterion Collection released (Wikidata's Criterion film id beside its TMDB id, weekly; the page address from Criterion's sitemap) pools its cover, the og:image of the Internet Archive's latest good copy of its criterion.com page (www.criterion.com challenges every non-browser client and its terms forbid automated collection, so it is never asked), labelled for the judge, whose prompt counts the Criterion logo and band as the edition's frame; lookups go one at a time, 4 s apart, and a found cover is kept for good. Archive: every applied title keeps each candidate at full size, its chosen poster and verdict.json under archive_dir (<kind>/<key>/, volume1 only: a run refuses the NVMe); unchanged files are never rewritten. taste_references_current adds references whose image is the title's current Plex poster, fetched once and cached. Every Wikimedia request is paced, 6.5 s apart without commons_contact (Wikimedia allows 10 a minute without a contact in the User-Agent). Gate: a dry run on the NAS over every collection lacking a poster, with a contact sheet of the chosen poster and the runner-up.
12 collections jellyfin/jf_mirror.py collections (never run) and the approved list in config/collections.approved.json Desired = the owner's 111 collections (config/collections.owner.json, frozen from the Plex export with their posters: a one-time migration) + the approved 150 + arrivals (TMDB collection, director, canon director at 3 films; facts from folder names and TMDB, never from an app). The apps are reconciled concurrently, each within its own budget on its own call timeout; a 5xx parks one collection, not the app; each app's item list is read once a day. NAS dry run lists every Plex and Jellyfin create/add/sort/poster; a real run limited to 3 approved franchises in Plex, verified through the API; a second run writes nothing.
13 health nothing (new) Table tests on every restart decision (threshold, cooldown, viewer veto, allow-list, curable failure), the restart sequence on a fake Docker API (stop grace, a start that never ran, a service that never answers, a refused stop, a shutdown), and a fake-server run. On the NAS: a read-only run prints every probe's result and latency. A restart is proven only on a throwaway container. Plex's Optimize Database: table tests on its triggers (3 slow runs, a load equal to plex_slow, a broken streak, 500 vs 501 changes, a 5xx, a 4xx) and on its hold (window ends, cooldown, a guest, an unread count), and one optimize's life on a fake Plex (refused, recorded before it is sent, followed in /activities, re-timed, still slow, cooldown, stuck). The NVMe volume (volume2): table tests on a fake mount table (missing, a plain folder, a read-only superblock behind the container's read-only bind, the fullness threshold, a stray entry), and in a throwaway container on the NAS with /volume2 bound read-only: no alert on the real volume, a stray entry named, a missing path and a plain folder alerted.
14 audit New (read-only library audit; replaces nothing) Table tests on every category and file-level naming rule. A move while the run reads the library (between a folder's listing and its read, after the walk, or into a folder already read) is never a finding or an alert, and such a run is not kept as the baseline. A probe killed on 3 runs in a row files the video as unreadable. On the NAS, read-only against the real library with the report in scratch: counts per category with examples, category 1 compared with the lead's leftover-folder count.
15 appbackup New (the NVMe app data had no backup) Over nightly runs on a fake clock: unchanged files hardlinked, a changed file of the same size copied, rows still in a live database's WAL in its copy and its -wal/-shm not, the transcode area excluded, a cut-off run's leftovers dropped, keep versions kept. On the NAS, on scratch copies of the real Plex databases: Plex's own SQLite reports integrity_check ok and searches the copy's tokenize=collating FTS table, which a stock SQLite cannot open; a second night hardlinks every unchanged file.

Order: small and independent stages first, so the pattern is proven before the rename stages. The shared probe/details work comes before the rename planner, because the planner consumes subtitle facts. The rename executor carries the most risk, so it waits until everything around it is in Go.

Build, ship, run

make test vet test-linux     # macOS + Linux; Linux exercises renameat2/FICLONE
make image                   # linux/amd64; Go cross-compiles natively, the runtime stage is emulated
make save                    # bin/projectionist-<ver>.tar.gz → NAS: docker load; Container Manager project = compose.yaml
projectionist run <stage>    # one run on the NAS (exit 1 on alert or error), for the gates above
